BOPEN.heard: Building virtual environments exam prep, key terms, pacing and guidance. Nineteen terms for steering the player, keeping a game fair and setting its rhythm from communication and anticipation to pacing and spacing. The exact term turns a vague complaint about a level into an instruction you can act on.

BIDEA.heard: Hollow, this is Liam in for bear. Newcomers often say that good pacing means the challenge keeps rising. That rise is progression. Pacing is the swing between intents and calm moments, a hard fight, and then a rest. A straight climb wears the player out. This film goes through the terms of guidance, fairness, and rhythm, each one shown, so you can name the exact one.

BDEFS.heard: Six labels sit in the corners of the pictures that follow. In the glossary, the term is on the course term list, but the text does not explain it. Video only, the term comes from a video lecture and is not in the course text or on the term list. Computed, the numbers are worked out on screen from stated inputs. Simulation, a model run step by step from stated rules, not a measurement of a real game. Illustrative data, numbers chosen to show the idea not measured. Conceptual, a drawing of the idea with no data behind it.

B0101.heard: This table is the map, 19 terms about game design in four groups. The first group is the foundation with the three pillars player purpose and communication. It covers what a game needs before anything else.

B0102.heard: The second group is Guiding the Player. Guiding the focus, linear and nonlinear, side quest level design, teaching through levels and design the middle first. These terms say how a player finds the way and learns the skills.

B0103.heard: The third group is meeting expectations. Anticipation, build up, logical events, consistent rules, and games can cheat. These terms say whether what happens in a game feels fair, sensible, and earned.

B0104.heard: The fourth group is rhythm and space, dynamic progression, pacing, waves and spacing. These terms say how much happens, how fast it happens, and where.

B0201.heard: This drawing is a building on three columns, and the first column player has risen in red. The three pillars are what a game rests on, the player's role, communication, and appeal. The first is player purpose, what the player does and why. The player, not the game, pushes things forward. For example, in a platformer like Walker, the purpose is to reach the goal flag, and every jump is the player's own choice.

B0202.heard: The second pillar communication now stands. Without it, the player does not know the goal or how to reach it and feels powerless. The box at the bottom sets it against player purpose. Purpose is what you do and why, and communication is showing you what and how. For example, a goal flag that waves at the far end of the first screen with a row of coins arching over the first gap shows a new player both.

B0203.heard: The third pillar appeal rises in red and the roof the game itself rests on all three. Appeal is the pull to keep playing. It is the hardest of the three to guarantee and the most important. For example, if your playdesters finish the first level and ask to play it again, it has appeal. If they put the controller down halfway, it may not.

B0301.heard: A room seen from above with a plain door on the far right. Communication means showing the player the goal and how to reach it with clues in the space itself. Here nothing marks the door. In this simulated run, the player wanders at random and needs 2,476 steps to find it. For example, a level that shows its goal flag on the first screen with a trail of coins pointing the way communicates the goal.

B0302.heard: Now the door is lit in red with a ring of light around it. Guiding the focus means making clear what the player should concentrate on right now. The same simulated player walks straight there in 43 steps. Communication tells the player the goal, and guiding the focus tells them where to look now. For example, when a new enemy drops into the level, the camera can pan to it for a moment, so the player looks at the threat.

B0401.heard: A chain of rooms from start to end. Linear and non-linear describe the route through a level. Linear means one route from start to end, each room opening onto the next. Here there is exactly one route. A linear level is easy to guide and the designer controls the pace. For example, a tutorial level where the player can only run right from the first platform to the goal flag is linear.

B0402.heard: Now the chain has two forks. Non-linear means the player chooses between routes. Each fork offers two ways through, so two times two gives four routes from start to end. For example, a level where the player picks a high path over the rooftops or a low path through the sewer and later picks again between a ladder and a lift is non-linear.

B0403.heard: Back to one main line with one red room off to the side. A side quest is a detour from the main storyline. It leaves the main line and returns to the same place so the main story still holds. That gives two ways to finish with the detour or without it. For example, a cave off the main path where the player can rescue a lost miner for a reward and then return to the road is a side quest.

B0501.heard: A red staircase climbs as the player learns skills along a famous first level, World 1-1. Level design is planning and building the spaces the player moves through. Teaching through levels means the first level lets the player try each skill with no text. Here seven skills are taught with no tutorial words. For example, level design places the floor, spikes, and goal flag of a walker level, and a level can teach by setting a small. Harmless gap before the first deadly one.

B0502.heard: A strip of three parts start middle and end with two orders under them. Design the middle first means building the engaging middle levels first, then the opening levels that take players there. The start is played first, but the middle, the red circle, is designed first. For example, you might build the hardest platform room of your game first, note which jumps it demands, then design the opening level to teach exactly those jumps.

B0601.heard: Two timelines of an enemy attack, one with no warning and one with a gray wind up before the red hit. Anticipation means preparing the player for what comes next. In this made up example with an assumed reaction time of a quarter of a second, a half second wind up leaves a quarter of a second to spare. No wind up leaves none and the hit feels cheap. For example, an enemy that crouches and flashes before it lunges gives the player anticipation.

B0602.heard: Three curves rise over the 10 seconds before an explosion, sound, sparks, and in red the camera shake. Build up is a sequence that raises tension toward an event. Anticipation is a short warning before one hit and buildup is a long rise. In these made up curves, the shake arrives last. For example, before a boss bursts through a wall, the music swells, dust falls from the ceiling, and the camera starts to tremble.

B0701.heard: A table of player actions and what happens next with ticks and crosses. Logical events means that what happens makes sense and meets the players on spoken expectations. Shoot a wall and a bullet hole appears. Walk on gravel and it crunches. In this made up table two of the four outcomes meet the expectation. For example, when the player's character lands in water, a splash sound and ripples should follow. A silent landing breaks the expectation.

B0702.heard: Two rows of bars show how high a ball bounces as a percent of the drop. Consistent rules means that even where a game bends physics it bends it the same way every time. In this made up example the dark row keeps 80% each time, 180, 64 and so on. The red row is random with no rule to learn. For example if your game gives the player a double jump, it should reach the same height on every level.

B0801.heard: A guard scene from above with a red cone where it looks and the player sneaking up behind. Games can cheat means hidden help the player does not notice. First, the honest version. In this simulation an honest guard senses all around it, turns at 120 pixels and the sneak fails. For example, a platformer that still lets the player jump for a split second after running off a ledge is cheating, and most players never notice.

B0802.heard: Now the guard is told not to turn. The player walks right up behind it and the game lets the ambush happen. That is the cheat and enemy ignoring what it could sense so the player's clever play is rewarded. It works only as long as the player does not notice. For example, the script of a patrolling enemy in a stealth level can skip its turn around whenever the player is right behind it.

B0901.heard: A timeline of four team actions in one round, throw smoke, flank, charge in and check angles all overlapping. Dynamic means many things happening at once, so play stays fresh. Here up to four things happen at the same moment, and the defenders must watch everything. For example, a boss fight where the boss swings at the player while small enemies drop in and the floor starts to crumble is dynamic.

B0902.heard: The same four actions now one after another. The round grows to 18 seconds and never more than one thing happens at a time. That is sequential play, the lookalike of dynamic. It is easy to predict and dull. For example, a boss that only swings, then only summons, then only shakes the floor. Each in turn gives the player one thing to watch at a time.

B1001.heard: A line of intensity climbs across 4 minutes past a grey comfortable band. Progression is the natural rise and challenge through a game. It should neither overstimulate nor understimulate the player. In these made up curves a straight climb stays in the band only 56% of the time and passes 0.8 near the end. For example a run of levels where each one adds a faster enemy, a wider gap or a new hazard has progression.

B1002.heard: Now the line swings up and down while its peaks still rise. Pacing means alternating intense and calm moments. In this made-up curve, the player stays in the band 88% of the time. Pacing is the swing between calm and intense, and progression is the overall rise. For example, a platformer level can follow a tight run of spikes with a quiet stretch and a checkpoint before the next hard jump.

B1003.heard: Two rows of enemy squares each one wave of total strength 10. Waves means a group of enemies sent together, many weak ones or a few strong ones. 10 enemies of strength 1 and 2 enemies of strength 5 add up to the same total, but the pressure feels different. For example, a tower defense level might send a swarm of small beetles in one wave, then two armored beetles in the next.

B1101.heard: A wide room seen from above with three characters drifting around it. Spacing means how open or tight the spaces of a level are, open areas to admire or tight ones that feel claustrophobic, with room left for enemies to move. In this simulated run each character gets 7 square meters and they touch in only 17 of 300 frames. For example, a wide cave with a view of a distant castle invites the player to stop and look.

B1102.heard: The same length of room, now one meter tall. Each character gets about 2.3 square meters, and in this simulated run they touch in 72 of 300 frames. Tight space is crowded, tense and claustrophobic and it changes the pace. For example, a narrow corridor where the player must slip past a patrolling enemy feels tense and the enemy needs room in it to turn around.

B1201.heard: Each pair sets two look alike terms side by side. Linear means one route from start to end, the room's in a row on the left. Non-linear means alternate routes the player picks, the fork on the right.

B1202.heard: Anticipation is a short warning just before an event, the gray bar before the red hit. Build up is a rise in tension toward the event, the long red curve. One is a moment, the other is sequence.

B1203.heard: Progression is the overall rise in challenge, the straight line on the left. Pacing is the swing between calm and intense, the wavy line on the right, which still rises as it swings.

B1204.heard: Logical events means things behave sensibly, so a shot wall gets a bullet hole. Consistent rules means bent physics is bent the same way every time. The dark bars shrink by a rule, and the red ones jump around.

B1301.heard: A vague request sits above the exact instruction that replaces it. Players keep getting lost becomes light the exit door and put a ring of light around it, visible from the start. In the simulated run steps to the door fall from 2476 to 43.

B1302.heard: The enemy hits feel cheap becomes at a half second wind up animation before every attack. With an assumed reaction time of a quarter of a second, no wind up leaves no time, and the wind up leaves a quarter of a second to spare.

B1303.heard: The level feels flat becomes alternate 60 seconds of enemies with 30 seconds of calm and send the strongest wave last. The chart shows peaks and rests that keep rising overall.

B1304.heard: The ending as a letdown becomes build up for 10 seconds with sound rising, sparks flying, and the camera shaking before the blast. The curve climbs slowly, then steeply.

B1305.heard: The physics feel random becomes bounces keep 80% of the height every time. 180, 64, and down. Each bounces 80% of the last, a rule the player can learn.

B1401.heard: This is a checklist of six questions to ask before you call the pacing done. First, does the player know their role, the goal, and how to reach it? That is player purpose and communication.

B1402.heard: Second, can the player tell where to look and do they have alternatives? That is guiding the focus in a non-linear route or a side quest.

B1403.heard: Third is every danger telegraphed shown before it strikes as anticipation asks, and do events behave as the player expects as logical events should.

B1404.heard: Fourth are the rules consistent bent the same way every time, and if the game cheats is the cheat hidden and does it help the player.

B1405.heard: Fifth, does the pace alternate and still rise inside a comfortable band? That is pacing and progression working together, calm and intense in turn on a line that keeps rising.

B1406.heard: Sixth is their room to move or is the space tight on purpose. Then say it exactly. Not the level feels flat, but 60 seconds of enemies, 30 seconds of calm.

BVDT.heard: Let's recap a game rests on three pillars the player communication and appeal. Communication shows the goal and guiding the focus shows where to look now. Linner has one route and non-linear lets the player choose between routes. Anticipation is a short warning and build up is a long rise in tension. Consistent rules bend physics the same way every time. Progression is the overall rise and pacing swings between calm and intense.

BHTF.heard: Quizmy on game design terms with short cases for making a platformer one at a time. Use the terms communication, guiding the focus, linear non-linear side quest, anticipation, build up, consistent rules, progression and pacing. For each case I must name the exact term and say why its look alike is wrong. Hold back the answer until I reply then tell me if I was right.

BOUT.heard: Key terms pacing and guidance at Nick Bear Brown.
